title: Evidence of Learned Look-Ahead in a Chess-Playing Neural Network
models: Leela Chess Zero policy network (15-layer, 109M-parameter transformer with one token per board square), used without MCTS
action_head: n/a (policy over chess moves; move logits from final source and target square embeddings)
methods: activation patching with corruptions chosen to change Leela's move but not a weaker model's
attention-head patching and targeted zero-ablation of single attention entries
identification of piece-movement heads and ablation of information flow out of future-move squares
bilinear probe for the move two turns ahead, with random-model control
question: Does a strong chess policy network internally represent and use future moves (look-ahead), or only state-based heuristics?
key_findings: On 22.5k filtered puzzles that Leela solves, patching activations on the target square of the 3rd move (two turns ahead) has an outsized effect on the best-move log odds in middle layers, while the 1st-move target dominates late layers.

Head L12H12 moves information from the 3rd-move target square to the 1st-move target square; zero-ablating that single attention entry (of about 1.5 million) strongly reduces performance on a substantial fraction of puzzles, while ablating all 4095 other entries of the head matters less.

Ablating information flow out of the 3rd-move target square in piece-movement heads for the relevant piece type reduces top-move log odds by at least 1.5 in 60% of puzzles; ablating other piece heads or a random square has little effect.
A bilinear probe motivated by L12H12 predicts the 3rd move with 92% accuracy, far above a probe on a randomly initialized model.
Results are stronger on puzzles where the 1st and 2nd move share a target square (83% of the filtered set, often sacrifices).

evidence.scale: 22.5k puzzles; 5 probe training runs; error bars as 2x SEM or 95% CIs
evidence.statistics: yes: standard errors and 95% CIs on patching, ablation and probe results
evidence.baselines: other squares, random squares, other piece-movement heads, probes on a random model

causal_validation: Yes: activation patching, single-entry attention ablations and head-specific ablations with matched controls show future-move squares are causally important for the output.
closed_loop: n/a (single-position policy evaluation, no sequential control)
limitations_stated: No precise description of how look-ahead is implemented.
Only a single line of play; no test of comparing multiple lines (search).
Focus on complex puzzle states; role across the full input distribution unclear.
Chess may favor look-ahead unusually strongly.
critique: Strong exemplar of convergent causal evidence (patching, ablation, probing with controls) that robotics interpretability papers rarely reach.

The token-per-square architecture makes 'where' a future move is represented directly interpretable; VLAs have no such alignment between tokens and action-relevant locations, which is a central obstacle the review should note.
Dataset filtering toward puzzles a weaker model fails and Leela solves selects for states where look-ahead is most likely, so prevalence of the mechanism is not established.
code: https://leela-interp.github.io/ (code on GitHub per the paper)
one_line: Activation patching, single-attention-entry ablations and a 92%-accurate probe show that Leela's chess policy network represents the optimal move two turns ahead on the relevant squares and uses it to choose its current move in hard puzzles.
